title: A Tulsa holiness revival and his wish to play a funeral
summary: With Henry Boyden's orchestra at a Tulsa tavern, Watts heard a holiness band swing spirituals, and says he has never played a funeral.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Well, now, I, uh, when I was in Lorton, Oklahoma, I was in Lorton, Oklahoma on a job at the Rock Tavern there. I just remember what year it was, but anyway, I was with Henry Boyden's orchestra. We had seven pieces and we played every night except Sunday, I think. And we used to make trips up to Tulsa in Oklahoma City, see, you know, on our off nights, you know. And we was broadcasting them, 15 minutes every evening on the radio for this rock tavern, but we played, see, nightly. And I went, I visited a holiness church in Tulsa, Arizona that seats about, oh, about 1,500 people. And at that time, they had a spiritual crusade going on, a revival in other words. And man, them people had seven pizzas up there on that pulpit every night. And man, you talking about playing. I don't know where the fellas come from. I never met them. I don't know if they're from Louisiana or New Orleans or where, but them fellas really was playing them, swinging those spirituals.

Yeah, you know, yeah, yeah. You know, for me not to recognize them as some of the old jazzmen, sidemen of the city, you know. They was really playing, man. I just got a kick just sitting there and just listening at them. And it's really to hear those hymns when they play it like that, you know. I see, Father. See, I'm telling you. That's why I always wanted to play a funeral and never have played when I'm 56 years old. Because I think when they're taking the body to the grave, ain't nothing could be sweeter than a brass band walking slow, playing those slow spirituals, you know.
